title: Control memory, concurrency, dependency, and platform-specific failures: decision comparison 1
teachingQuestion: Which implementation failure violates the security invariant—memory safety, concurrency, resource limit, dependency behavior, or programmable policy—and what layered evidence detects it?
focalInsight: Memory safety/buffer bounds, race/concurrency invariants, resource exhaustion, dependency change, software-defined control-plane security.
caption: Compare meaning, decision conditions, and failures. These concise distinctions are paired with the worked examples in the teaching unit.

nodes.label: Memory Safety
nodes.definition: The property that software accesses memory only within valid bounds, lifetime, type, and ownership rules.
nodes.decision: Prefer safe constructs/languages where suitable and enforce bounds/lifetime discipline; test unsafe interfaces and treat mitigations as layers.
nodes.failureExample: Use-after-free or out-of-bounds access can corrupt data or transfer control to attacker-influenced code.
nodes.detail: The property that software accesses memory only within valid bounds, lifetime, type, and ownership rules.

nodes.label: Buffer Overflow
nodes.definition: Writing more data than a fixed buffer can hold, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially altering behavior or control flow.
nodes.decision: Validate/bound input and use safe APIs/structures/compiler/runtime protections; test edge and oversized input at every interface.
nodes.failureExample: A 17th byte written into a 16-byte buffer can overwrite adjacent state.
nodes.detail: Writing more data than a fixed buffer can hold, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially altering behavior or control flow.

nodes.label: Race Condition
nodes.definition: A defect where correctness or security outcome depends on uncontrolled timing/interleaving of concurrent operations.
nodes.decision: Define the invariant, use synchronization/atomicity/idempotency as appropriate, and test forced interleavings and duplicate requests.
nodes.failureExample: Two withdrawals both see available funds before either update, violating the balance invariant.
nodes.detail: A defect where correctness or security outcome depends on uncontrolled timing/interleaving of concurrent operations.

nodes.label: Concurrency
nodes.definition: Execution of multiple tasks whose shared state, ordering, visibility, cancellation, and failures must be controlled.
nodes.decision: Choose coordination that preserves required integrity/authorization semantics and bound retries/timeouts.
nodes.failureExample: Parallel requests can bypass a single-use token rule if check and consume are not atomic.
nodes.detail: Execution of multiple tasks whose shared state, ordering, visibility, cancellation, and failures must be controlled.

nodes.label: Resource Exhaustion
nodes.definition: Loss of availability when requests, memory, CPU, files, connections, retries, or queues consume finite resources without adequate bounds.
nodes.decision: Apply quotas, timeouts, cancellation, backpressure, size/rate limits, and resilient failure handling based on service need.
nodes.failureExample: Unbounded file upload processing can exhaust workers and deny legitimate users service.
nodes.detail: Loss of availability when requests, memory, CPU, files, connections, retries, or queues consume finite resources without adequate bounds.

nodes.label: Dependency Risk
nodes.definition: Risk introduced when a library, runtime, platform, or policy dependency changes, is vulnerable, unsupported, malicious, or behaves unexpectedly.
nodes.decision: Inventory/pin/review dependencies, assess update impact, test changes, and retain rollback/response ownership.
nodes.failureExample: A library update can change authorization defaults even if application source did not change.
nodes.detail: Risk introduced when a library, runtime, platform, or policy dependency changes, is vulnerable, unsupported, malicious, or behaves unexpectedly.

nodes.label: Software Defined Security
nodes.definition: Security capabilities whose policy, enforcement, configuration, or control plane is programmable and distributed across software-managed infrastructure/services.
nodes.decision: Protect policy authorship/approval, validate changes, separate duties, stage/monitor rollout, log decisions, define safe failure, and retain rollback.
nodes.failureExample: A compromised policy service can rapidly grant broad access across every connected workload.
nodes.detail: Security capabilities whose policy, enforcement, configuration, or control plane is programmable and distributed across software-managed infrastructure/services.

learningContract.teachingQuestion: Which implementation failure violates the security invariant—memory safety, concurrency, resource limit, dependency behavior, or programmable policy—and what layered evidence detects it?
learningContract.misconception: A compiler/runtime mitigation or central policy engine guarantees correct authorization, integrity, and availability.
learningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
learningContract.focalInsight: Memory safety/buffer bounds, race/concurrency invariants, resource exhaustion, dependency change, software-defined control-plane security.
learningContract.intentionalOmissions: Do not prescribe a language, locking primitive, quota value, policy engine, or make toolchain mitigations absolute guarantees.
learningContract.retrievalPrompt: Two transfers race for the same balance after a policy change. State the invariant, enforcement, test evidence, and safe rollback/failure behavior.
